passage:
Wednesday night.
Tejas again today. Third time this week he said "those people" with that face, like he'd bitten something rotten. His phone is only one channel now. He skipped cricket and Ravi's birthday. He used to be the one who organised everything.
I wanted to argue. I had facts ready. Instead I asked, "What's been going on with you, really?"
He was quiet, then it came out. The scholarship was cut in June. His father's shop is struggling. He feels like nobody listens to people like him. The channel "at least says it out loud."
I didn't agree with the channel. I just said, "That sounds exhausting. I'm sorry nobody listened."
He actually looked at me.
Later, with his okay, I messaged Mr Rao, the college counsellor. He replied tonight: "Thank you. Tell Tejas my door is open tomorrow at eleven, and you can come with him if he likes."
Zainab

qa.a: Tejas may have felt seen for the first time in months, which is why he actually looked at Zainab.

Every evening Ganga and Deepika used to walk to the canal after tailoring class in Sonpur. Lately Deepika walked with earphones in, the same channel playing, and when they passed the boys from across the river she muttered, "Filth. All of them." She had stopped coming to class. She had stopped laughing at Ganga's jokes.
Ganga's first wish was to argue. Instead she sat down on the canal wall and asked, "What's hurting, Deepu?"
Deepika was silent a long time. Then it came out: her engagement had been broken off in March, the whole village had talked, and her father had stopped speaking to her. "At least these videos say it's not my fault. They say it's their fault."
Ganga didn't correct her. She held her hand and listened until dark. Walking back, she said, "Didi from the women's group at the panchayat helped my cousin once. Will you come with me to see her tomorrow?"
Deepika nodded.

qa.a: Her engagement had been broken off in March.

qa.a: Ganga felt frustrated and worried enough to argue, but chose to sit on the canal wall and ask what was hurting.

qa.a: Ganga listened to the pain underneath without correcting her, then offered to go together to the didi from the panchayat women's group.

qa.q: How does Deepika explain why the videos appeal to her?
qa.a: Deepika feels blamed and cut off after the broken engagement, and the videos tell her it's not her fault but someone else's.

At the adult evening college in Porto, Lucia had taught Dalia for two terms. Dalia used to argue cheerfully about every poem. This spring she arrived late, earbuds in, one channel's videos filling her phone. In a class discussion about migration she said, "They're not people, they're an invasion," and two classmates went silent.
Lucia felt her face heat up. She wanted to argue right there. She didn't. After class she asked Dalia to stay and help stack chairs.
"You seem angry lately," Lucia said. "Not at me. Just angry."
Dalia folded her arms, then unfolded them. Her mother's café had closed in the winter. She had been working nights. "Nobody cares about people like us," she said. "Those videos do."
Lucia listened. She didn't mention the channel once. At the end she said, "I'd like you to meet Marta, our student counsellor. She's good with the angry stuff. Tomorrow at four?"
"Maybe," Dalia said, and helped with the last chair.

qa.q: What happened to Dalia's mother's café?
qa.a: Her mother's café had closed in the winter.

qa.q: What did Lucia feel after Dalia's comment in class, and what did Lucia do with it?
qa.a: Lucia felt her face heat up with anger and wanted to argue, but held back and asked Dalia to stay and stack chairs.

qa.q: How did Lucia keep Dalia's trust while getting help?
qa.a: Lucia named the anger kindly, listened without mentioning the channel, and offered a meeting with Marta, the student counsellor, the next day.

qa.q: What does 'Those videos do' show about Dalia's pull toward the channel?
qa.a: Dalia feels ignored and worn out after the café closed and the night work, and the videos seem to be the only ones who care.

The college athletics club changing room smelled of liniment. Nazia, the club captain, was taping her wrist when she heard Shankar on the bench laughing at a video. "Look at them. Animals. Should all be thrown out." Two first-years edged away.
Shankar had skipped four practices. He used to stay late to help juniors with their starts. Now he sat alone at meals, earbuds in, the same furious channel.
Nazia didn't snap at him. After practice she sat on the bench, one space away. "You've missed a lot. I'm not here to argue. What's going on?"
He shrugged. Then, after a while, it came out: his scholarship had been cut after the injury, and his family back home thought he'd wasted it. "At least the guy in the videos says it's not us who failed."
Nazia nodded slowly. "That sounds heavy to carry alone. Coach Pillai knows the scholarship office. Can I walk you over to him now?"
Shankar looked at her a long moment, then stood up.

qa.a: Shankar had skipped four practices.

qa.a: She took the pain seriously and offered to walk Shankar to Coach Pillai at once, linking the grievance to someone who can actually help.

passage:
Dear Ms Fernandes,
I'm writing about my friend Jatin, second-year mechanical, with his permission.
Over the last four months he has changed a lot. He used to joke with everyone in our hostel wing. Now he talks about "those people" with real contempt, calls whole groups parasites, and watches only one channel late into the night. He has stopped coming to Sunday football and left our old group chat.
At first I argued with him, and he just stopped talking to me. Last week I tried something else. I asked how he was really doing. He told me his father lost his job at the mill in March and the family might lose the house. He said the channel was the only place that explained why. I just listened. I didn't agree, and I didn't fight.
He has agreed to come and see you with me on Thursday at 4. I think he needs someone who can take his anger seriously and help him with it.
Thank you,
Pema

qa.q: What happened to Jatin's father in March?
qa.a: He lost his job at the mill.

qa.q: What seems to lie under Pema's choice to listen instead of argue?
qa.a: Pema felt concerned and hurt when arguing made Jatin stop talking, so chose patience to keep his trust.

qa.q: Why was listening a wiser step than arguing?
qa.a: Listening reached the pain beneath the contempt, the lost job and the house, and kept enough trust for Jatin to agree to see the counsellor.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel about the channel's explanations?
qa.a: Jatin likely feels scared and angry about his family's troubles, and the channel gives him someone to blame, which feels like an answer.
